layers.name: Energy
layers.description: Electricity is the foundation. Generation, storage and a stronger grid turn ambition into dependable power.
layers.connection: Reliable electricity powers chips. Grid connections and cooling determine where infrastructure can grow.
layers.outlook: Track new generation, grid delivery and demand together. More annual energy does not automatically provide power in the right place at the right time.

layers.name: Chips
layers.description: Accelerators, advanced memory and packaging transform electricity into compute. Manufacturing turns better designs into real supply.
layers.connection: Chips draw on energy and become useful at scale when infrastructure connects, powers and cools them.
layers.outlook: Follow operational fabs and reproducible system benchmarks. Process-node names alone do not establish speed, efficiency or available AI capacity.

layers.name: Infrastructure
layers.description: Data centers, networking and cooling bring individual processors together into systems that can train and serve AI.
layers.connection: Infrastructure joins energy and chips into usable capacity, making model training and inference possible.
layers.outlook: Follow projects from announcement through financing, construction and operation. Site counts and investment pledges are context, not delivered compute.

layers.name: Models
layers.description: Models convert compute into useful capabilities: reasoning, language, science and understanding the physical world.
layers.connection: Models use infrastructure to learn and respond. Lower costs and stronger reliability unlock more applications.
layers.outlook: Track capability, reliability, cost and openness separately. Better benchmark scores need to translate into dependable performance in real tasks.

layers.name: Applications
layers.description: AI becomes valuable through what people do with it: better tools, scientific discovery, more productive work and new possibilities.
layers.connection: Applications turn model capability into practical outcomes and create demand throughout the layers below.
layers.outlook: Look beyond adoption toward demonstrated outcomes. Practical value depends on the task, implementation and people using the technology.

metrics.title: Global data-center electricity demand
metrics.scope: All data centers, including non-AI workloads. Annual electricity consumption; not generation capacity.
metrics.note: 2024 is the 2025 report baseline; 2025 and 2030 use the updated 2026 IEA outlook. The 2030 value is a forecast, not a generation target.

metrics.title: U.S. data-center electricity demand
metrics.scope: All U.S. data centers. 2028 is a modeled range from the 2024 report, retained as a historical forecast vintage.
metrics.note: The 2028 interval is 325–580 TWh. A newer LBNL update exists; this series remains explicitly dated until reviewed.

metrics.title: U.S. nuclear capacity ambition
metrics.scope: Total U.S. nuclear generating capacity across the economy; not allocated to AI.
metrics.note: DOE describes an approximately 100 GW starting fleet and a 400 GW goal for 2050. The starting point is not a current progress measurement.

metrics.title: TSMC annual manufacturing capacity
metrics.scope: All TSMC-managed facilities and subsidiaries; includes non-AI chips and mature processes.
metrics.note: Company-reported capacity exceeds 17 million wafers in 2025. This measures manufacturing context, not AI accelerator shipments.

metrics.title: U.S. data-center footprint
metrics.scope: Stanford AI Index 2026 reported count of U.S. data centers; all types, not AI-only facilities.
metrics.note: A site count describes geographic footprint. It does not measure operational MW, utilization or installed AI compute. Period is the report vintage (2026).

metrics.title: Microsoft Wisconsin investment commitments
metrics.scope: Wisconsin data-center investment pledges; initial facility and additional second facility. Not recognized expenditure.
metrics.note: The September 2025 announcement adds $4B over three years to the initial $3.3B pledge. Completion and actual expenditure require subsequent evidence.

metrics.title: The falling cost of useful intelligence
metrics.scope: Cost of querying a model at GPT-3.5-equivalent MMLU performance, as defined by Stanford AI Index 2025.
metrics.note: Two historical price observations at a comparable benchmark threshold. These are not current provider prices or a universal capability measure.

metrics.title: AI use is becoming part of everyday work
metrics.scope: Organizations reporting AI use in at least one business function, as summarized by Stanford AI Index from survey evidence. Not population-wide adoption.
metrics.note: Survey-based adoption across annual report vintages; sampling and methodology may change. Adoption is distinct from measured productivity or return on investment.

targets.title: Plan for global data-center electricity demand
targets.detail: Demand projection for all data centers. A matched generation-and-grid delivery series is needed to assess readiness.

targets.title: Expand U.S. nuclear generating capacity
targets.detail: Economy-wide target. The approximate starting fleet is not a current measurement of additions toward the goal.

targets.title: Build a second Wisconsin data center
targets.detail: Three-year spending pledge. We need subsequent expenditure and commissioning evidence before assessing delivery.
